sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Break the word into pieces like building blocks: 'hepat' is the piece for liver, and '-itis' always means swollen and irritated. Put them together and you get an inflamed liver. The other words use the liver piece too, but with endings that mean 'big,' 'tumor,' or 'poisonous' instead.

### Question 2

Think of 'gastric juice' in your stomach after a big meal, or a 'gastro bug' that upsets your tummy. That 'gastro' part always points to the stomach. Other parts of the food tube get their own labels, so the stomach keeps 'gastr/o' as its own name tag.

### Question 3

Picture '-ectomy' as the word 'EXIT' with scissors: whatever comes before it gets cut out and shown the door. So appendectomy means the appendix is taken out. The look-alike endings mean making a doorway (-ostomy), taking a peek (-scopy), or fixing something (-plasty) instead.

### Question 4

The gallbladder is a little sac that holds bile, so its name literally means 'bile-sac' (chol/e for bile, cyst for sac). Put them together as 'cholecyst' and add '-itis' for swollen, and you get an inflamed bile-sac. The liver is a different organ with its own name, hepat, so it never gets mixed in here.

### Question 5

Same colon, two different endings that do very different jobs. '-ostomy' is like installing a new door in a wall so waste has a fresh exit, while '-ectomy' is like tearing out a section of the wall entirely. One adds an opening, the other takes tissue away.

### Question 6

'dys-' is the 'something's-not-working-right' prefix, like a bike with a bent wheel. '-phagia' is about swallowing food down. Put them together and the trip from mouth to stomach is bumpy. Watch out for its twin '-phasia,' which sounds almost the same but means speech - so 'dysphasia' is trouble talking, not trouble swallowing.

### Question 7

You can stack organ name-tags in one word like train cars. Start with the small-intestine car ('enter') and hook a stomach car ('gastr/o') in front, and now the word covers both stops. The '-itis' ending still means swollen and irritated.

### Question 8

'-scopy' is the 'let's-take-a-look' ending, like using a flashlight to peek inside a tunnel. A colonoscopy sends a tiny camera down the colon to look around, not to cut, patch, or add a door. So the word tells you it was a looking job.

### Question 9

'-megaly' is in the same family as 'mega' and 'megaphone,' which all mean big. So whatever organ sits in front of it has grown too large. Hepat is the liver and splen is the spleen, so both organs are oversized here, not removed or inflamed.

### Question 10

Read it in chunks: 'chol/e' is bile, 'lith' is stone (like a monolith is a big stone), and '-iasis' means 'there is a condition of having these.' So the word says there are stones made in the bile system, aka gallstones. No cutting, no swelling, just stones present.

### Question 11

Same bile neighborhood, three different addresses. 'Chol/e-lith-iasis' just says stones are present in the bile system (gallstones). 'Choledoch/o' is the name for the common bile duct, so 'choledocholithiasis' pins the stone to that specific pipe. 'Cholecyst' is the bile-sac (gallbladder), and '-itis' means swollen, so 'cholecystitis' is an inflamed gallbladder, not a stone at all.

### Question 12

These three sound liver-related but do different jobs. 'Hepatitis' is a build-it word meaning the liver is swollen. 'Cirrhosis' is a special name for a liver that has turned scarred and stiff over time. 'Jaundice' is not about naming the organ at all; it is the yellow color you see in the skin and eyes when bile pigment backs up. Same neighborhood, three different meanings.
